timecoded_text_to_speech.text: This is the aluminum battery we have. It's made of aluminum and graphite. Both materials are quite cheap.
Right now it's lighting up LED light and you can bend it and still you can see the LED light is still on while you are bending it.
Similarly as this we have two batteries with a cell phone so it can provide like 5V and it can be charged within a minute.
It's possible to have like bendable cell phone with bendable screen. You have bendable batteries on the back and it's great.
This is a DCM ion battery which we use a lot in our daily lives. For example in our cell phone and in our laptops.
Commonly DCM ion battery if you drill a hole through the battery or like probably catch on fire but our aluminum battery is non-flammable.
So if you drill the hole through it it's still running for a while. It's definitely a high safety battery we have.
It has a reasonable capacity and a very long cycle life. It has no decay over hundreds of cycles even thousands of cycles.
So you can have a potential application in like a great scale electric storage. So it's quite exciting.
I think it can be further improved and this is a great start. We think that it has a bright future.

youtube_description:
Stanford University Professor Hongjie Dai and colleagues have developed the first high-performance aluminum battery that’s fast charging, long lasting and inexpensive. The flexible, non-flammable device produces 2 volts of electricity. The research team was able to generate 5 volts - enough to power a smartphone - using two aluminum batteries and a converter.

In this video, graduate student Ming Gong and postdoctoral scholar Yingpeng Wu demonstrate how the new technology could offer a safe alternative to lithium-ion and other batteries in wide use today. 

Producer: Mark Shwartz, Precourt Institute for Energy, Stanford

Date: April 3, 2015

MORE INFORMATION:
https://energy.stanford.edu/news/aluminum-battery-stanford-offers-safe-alternative-conventional-batteries

Nature magazine (April 16, 2015):
http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v520/n7547/full/nature14340.html

Dai Laboratory: http://dailab.stanford.edu/

Precourt Institute for Energy: https://energy.stanford.edu/
